title: 2009 HMMT February Calculus Problem 1
statement: Let \(f\) be a differentiable real-valued function defined on the positive real numbers. The tangent lines to the graph of \(f\) always meet the \(y\)-axis 1 unit lower than where they meet the function. If \(f(1)=0\), what is \(f(2)\) ?

solutions.text: The tangent line to \(f\) at \(x\) meets the \(y\)-axis at \(f(x)-1\) for any \(x\), so the slope of the tangent line is \(f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{1}{x}\), and so \(f(x)=\ln (x)+C\) for some \(a\). Since \(f(1)=0\), we have \(C=0\), and so \(f(x)=\ln (x)\). Thus \(f(2)=\ln (2)\).
